plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single plot tracing the flight path of a batted ball across a distance-versus-height grid. The horizontal axis is labeled "Distance (ft)" and runs from 0 to 600 with ticks every 100 feet; the vertical axis is labeled "Height (ft)" and carries labeled ticks at 100, 200, and 300, with faint dotted gridlines filling the plotting area. A teal curve leaves the origin, climbs as a broad downward-opening parabola to a maximum slightly above 150 feet near a distance of about 290 feet, then falls back to the horizontal axis a little past 560 feet, with small arrowheads spaced along its length showing the direction of travel. A leader line labeled "Position of hitter" points to the curve's start at the origin, and a second leader labeled "Trajectory of ball" points to a small circular marker on the rising branch near 200 feet. A short red rectangle stands on the horizontal axis at 400 feet and is labeled "Outfield wall"; the curve passes far above its top. Setting the wall directly beneath the arc invites the reader to compare the ball's height at that distance against the height of the barrier. The plot renders a projectile path in a form that settles whether the hit clears the wall.

interactions.label: Distance from hitter (ft)
interactions.teaches: Each horizontal distance corresponds to exactly one height on the arc, so the trajectory is a function height(distance); dragging the marker makes the (distance, height) pair and the vertical drop to the ground concrete.

interactions.label: Outfield wall position (ft)
interactions.teaches: Whether the hit is a home run is decided at a single x-value: compare the ball's height on the curve to the fixed wall height at the wall's distance — above means it clears, below means it is caught.

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The same projectile motion can be read as a continuous curve or as a table of discrete (distance, height) samples — the smooth arc is just the connected version of those sample points.

demo_steps.title: Read the trajectory
demo_steps.narration: The teal arc leaves the hitter at the origin, climbs to a peak of about 155 ft near 290 ft, and lands near 560 ft; the arrowheads show the ball's direction of travel.

demo_steps.title: Height at a distance
demo_steps.narration: Drag the distance marker along the arc: the vertical drop line and height readout update, showing that every distance has exactly one height — the path is a function.

demo_steps.title: Clearing the wall
demo_steps.narration: Move the wall slider: at 400 ft the ball is far above the short red wall, but slide the wall toward the landing point and the curve dips below the wall height, turning a home run into an out.

demo_steps.title: Curve versus samples
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to sampled points: the same arc appears as discrete (distance, height) dots on the grid, connecting the smooth graph to a table of values.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A projectile path is a height-versus-distance function, so 'does it clear the wall?' is nothing more than comparing two heights — the curve's and the wall's — at one horizontal distance.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Standard 2D plot: x-axis 0–600 labeled 'Distance (ft)' with ticks every 100, y-axis 0–300 labeled 'Height (ft)' with ticks at 100/200/300, faint dotted gridlines. Teal parabola through (0,0), vertex ≈(290,155), root ≈(560,0), with small teal arrowheads along it. A small open circular marker sits on the rising branch near (200,140) with a leader line 'Trajectory of ball'; another leader 'Position of hitter' points to the origin. A short solid red rectangle (fixed wall height ≈20 ft) stands on the x-axis, default at 400 ft, labeled 'Outfield wall'. The distance marker is a highlighted dot with a dashed vertical drop line and a numeric height readout; the wall comparison highlight tints green when ball height > wall height and red otherwise. In 'Sampled points' mode replace the smooth stroke with evenly spaced teal dots (e.g. every 40 ft) on the same parabola.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for distance from the hitter: the learner drags a marker along the trajectory, the height readout and vertical drop to the x-axis update, and the parabola's height-at-distance relationship becomes concrete.
- Slider for outfield wall position: the learner moves the wall left or right, the figure highlights whether the ball is above or below the wall at that distance, and clearing the wall becomes a comparison of two heights at one x-value.

authoredContext:
The ball is 141.8 feet in the air when it soars out of the ballpark. It was indeed a home run. See the figure.

Plotted trajectory of a hit ball, showing the position of the batter at the origin, the ball's path in the shape of a wide downward facing parabola, and the outfield wall as a vertical line segment rising to 10 ft under the ball's path.
